name: Colombo
title: Colombo guide — Bawa’s house, Port City, where to stay | Ceylon Hop
description: What to do in Colombo beyond a stopover — Bawa’s house, Port City, street art, sunset on Marine Drive, where to eat, drink and stay, and how we drive you there.

hero.intro: Sri Lanka’s capital and biggest city, and the first and last place most visitors see. Dutch and British buildings between new towers, a harbour-front district rising out of the sea, temples by the lake and sunsets over the Indian Ocean — with the right picks, worth exploring in its own right.

lede: Most people give Colombo a night or two, at the start or the end of the trip —
ledeEm: pick well and it’s a stop worth having, not just somewhere to get through.

gettingHere.heading: We’ll bring you into Colombo
gettingHere.sub: Hotel to hotel, fixed price, one driver who knows the road. From wherever you are.

origins.title: Straight from the airport
origins.from: CMB · 35 km · about 50 min · most of it on the expressway
origins.sell: Your driver meets you at arrivals and takes the airport expressway into the city. Rush hour can stretch it to an hour or more, so tell us your flight and we’ll plan around it.

origins.title: From Kandy
origins.from: 125 km · about 3 h 30 · down from the hills
origins.sell: Down the old Kandy road through the low country, past the cashew sellers of Cadjugama. The new expressway won’t be finished before 2028, so this is still the way. We can stop for cashews if you’d like.

origins.title: From Galle
origins.from: 135 km · about 2 h 15 · up the Southern Expressway
origins.sell: Most of the way on the expressway, through paddy and rubber country. Want the sea instead? The old coast road takes about 3 hours and passes Kalutara’s white temple — just ask.

gettingHere.train:
The coastal line between Colombo and Galle is running normally. It’s the one worth taking: sit on the right going south for the sea, and on the left coming back. Reserved seats are sold only on seatreservation.railway.gov.lk — you need every passenger’s passport number when you book, and the original passport on the train.

The Kandy line still isn’t running through. Since Cyclone Ditwah, trains from Colombo go only as far as Rambukkana. The railway expects to reopen it in stages, but a bridge just outside Kandy is still being repaired, so check before you plan. Message us and we’ll check for your date — and drive you if it’s not running.

places.name: Gangaramaya & Beira Lake
places.text: Gangaramaya is a busy working temple by Beira Lake, with a museum and row upon row of Buddha statues — calm enough for children, and a gentle first taste of Buddhist Sri Lanka. Seema Malakaya, a short walk away, is Geoffrey Bawa’s 1979 pavilion that seems to float on the lake, and swan pedal boats go out from the shore nearby.

spec.open: About 6 AM–10 PM · Seema Malakaya to 9 PM
spec.ticket: ≈ Rs 500, one ticket for both · cash

tip.text: Cover shoulders and knees, shoes off, and never pose with your back to a Buddha — it’s taken seriously here. Colombo City Centre mall is a short walk away if you want air-conditioning and shops afterwards. If a friendly stranger says there’s a special festival today and waves down a tuk-tuk, smile and walk on: that ride ends at a gem shop.

places.name: Green Path & Viharamahadevi Park
places.text: Along Ananda Coomaraswamy Mawatha, opposite Viharamahadevi Park, local artists hang their canvases on the railings — an open-air gallery of landscapes, portraits and pop art. Walk it, then cross into the park, Colombo’s oldest and largest, under the shade of the big trees.

spec.open: Most days · best at weekends, about 11 AM–6 PM

tip.text: Prices are there to be talked about — a smile and a counter-offer are expected. Small canvases roll up for the flight home.

places.name: Number 11, Geoffrey Bawa’s house
places.text: The Colombo home of Sri Lanka’s most famous architect: four small bungalows down a quiet lane, joined into one house of courtyards, light wells and found objects. Now a small museum of his tropical modernism, seen on a guided tour.

spec.open: Tours Mon–Fri 10 AM, 2 & 3:30 PM · Sat 11 AM & 4 PM · Sun 11 AM

tip.text: Tours only, and places go first come, first served — book ahead through geoffreybawa.com. Pair it with Seema Malakaya on Beira Lake, Bawa’s too.

places.name: Street art in Slave Island
places.text: Murals tucked into the back lanes near Slave Island station, many painted with the people who live there and telling the neighbourhood’s own story — the #WeAreFromHere project began here in 2018. One of the oldest parts of Colombo, and changing fast.

spec.from: Slave Island · a few minutes from the Fort

tip.text: The old neighbourhood is being redeveloped and some walls have already come down — ask us what’s still standing before you go. Late afternoon has the best light and cooler air. These are people’s homes: ask before photographing anyone.

places.name: Pettah: the Red Mosque & the Dutch Museum
places.text: Colombo at full volume: market lanes piled with fabric, spices and gadgets. In the middle stands Jami Ul-Alfar, the Red Mosque, striped red and white like a stick of rock — free, with a guide from the mosque to show you round. On Prince Street, the Dutch Period Museum fills a 17th-century mansion with the city’s Dutch colonial story.

spec.open: Mosque 9:30 AM–5:30 PM · Fridays from 3 PM
spec.ticket: Mosque free · museum a small fee

tip.text: Go before ten, ahead of the heat and the crush, and keep your phone and wallet in front of you. At the mosque, use gate 3 and dress modestly — women need a headscarf. The museum’s hours have changed since it reopened, so we’ll check for your day. Opposite the mosque, Bombay Sweet Mahal does samosas and Indian sweets.

places.name: Lotus Tower
places.text: The pink-and-green spire you can see from all over the city — South Asia’s tallest, with an observation deck about 240 m above sea level. Go after dark, when Colombo lights up below you and the tower glows. Twenty minutes at the top is plenty for most people.

spec.open: Tickets 9 AM–9 PM · weekends to 10 PM
spec.ticket: USD 20 adult · USD 10 age 3–10 · plus VAT, paid in rupees

tip.text: Book a time slot on the official site, colombolotustower.lk — tickets can’t be refunded or transferred. Bring your passport: it’s checked at the door. An evening slot is the one worth paying for.

places.name: Port City: karts, scooters & the water
places.text: A new district built on land reclaimed from the sea, next to Galle Face. Ride an e-scooter along the waterfront promenades, race a few laps of the SpeedBay go-kart circuit, or head to The Clubhouse for jet skis, kayaks, paddle boards and banana rides.

spec.open: Karts Wed–Sun 4–10 PM · water sports daily 10 AM–8:30 PM
spec.ticket: Karts ≈ USD 26 for 10 min · scooters from ≈ Rs 500

tip.text: Book the karts ahead, and come in the late afternoon: race or ride as it cools, then stay for sunset on the promenade.

places.name: Marine Drive at sunset
places.text: The long seafront road from Kollupitiya down to Wellawatte, where locals walk, jog and fish off the rocks as the sun drops into the sea — far less crowded than Galle Face Green. Galle Face itself is a short ride north, for kites, food carts and isso vadai.

tip.text: The coastal railway runs between the road and the sea, and trains come often — cross only at a crossing, and look both ways. Tell your driver which end you’re starting from and we’ll put you on the sea side.

places.name: Green Colombo: wetlands & parks
places.text: Boardwalks through the city’s wetlands, a short drive out: Diyasaru Park and Beddagana for birds, monitor lizards and, at Diyasaru, fishing cats in a large enclosure; the 3 km Bellanwila cycle track beside its marsh, with bikes to rent; and Diyatha Uyana’s riverside paths and stalls. The best of it for children.

spec.ticket: Diyasaru Rs 500 foreign adult · the rest free or a small fee

tip.text: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the birds are out and it’s cooler. Bring insect repellent.

places.name: A rainy afternoon: bowling, pottery or paint
places.text: For a wet day or a family that needs a break from sightseeing: Playdium in One Galle Face Mall has bowling, an arcade, bumper cars, a VR zone and karaoke. Or make something — a 90-minute pottery session at L’Atelier de Sabine, or a sip-and-paint evening at Tipsy Da Vinci’s.

spec.open: Playdium about 10 AM–10 PM · classes by booking
spec.ticket: Playdium per activity · pottery ≈ Rs 3,500 · paint ≈ Rs 6,500

tip.text: Pottery pieces need three to four weeks to be fired, so it works best if you’re staying in Sri Lanka a while — or just enjoy the wheel. Message the studios ahead; classes fill up.

furtherAfield.name: Negombo
furtherAfield.text: The beach town by the airport: a fish market where the catch dries on the sand, St Mary’s Church and the old Dutch canal. Handy for your last night before an early flight.

furtherAfield.name: Kelaniya Raja Maha Vihara
furtherAfield.text: A big working temple about 11 km north-east of the centre, with Solias Mendis’s murals of the Buddha’s past lives inside. No foreigner ticket — a donation is welcome. Shoulders and knees covered.

furtherAfield.name: Bentota & the Madu River
furtherAfield.text: A mangrove river of 64 islands, explored by boat in about an hour, with Bevis Bawa’s Brief Garden and Geoffrey Bawa’s Lunuganga close by. Best as a stop on the way to Galle, not a day trip there and back.

itinerary.heading: A plan that works
itinerary.sub: Two easy days in the city, in the order that beats the heat and the traffic — then on down the coast, or up to the hills.

days.title: Day 1 · Temples, high tea and a rooftop
days.sub: An easy first day, then the city by night

steps.title: Gangaramaya & Seema Malakaya
steps.text: Before the heat. Cover up for the temple.

steps.title: Colombo City Centre
steps.text: A short walk away, for shopping in the air-conditioning.

steps.title: Lunch at Green Cabin
steps.text: Rice and curry, or the lamprais it’s known for.

steps.title: High tea at ITC Ratnadipa
steps.text: Five minutes from the mall — book a table.

steps.title: Sunset on Marine Drive
steps.text: Or Galle Face Green for isso vadai from the carts.

steps.title: Dinner, then a rooftop bar
steps.text: ON14 at the Radisson for the view. Book at weekends.

days.title: Day 2 · Bawa, Port City and Park Street
days.sub: One choice in the morning, then the waterfront

steps.title: Number 11, or Diyasaru Park
steps.text: Bawa’s house on the 10 AM tour — or the wetland boardwalks if you’re with children.

steps.title: Pettah & the Dutch Museum
steps.text: The Red Mosque and lunch at Bombay Sweet Mahal.

steps.title: Port City
steps.text: Go-karts (Wed–Sun) or an e-scooter along the promenade.

steps.title: Park Street Mews
steps.text: Restaurants and bars in old warehouses, live music most nights.

steps.title: On down the coast with us
steps.text: About 2 h 15 to Galle on the expressway — or up to Kandy, or straight to the airport.

months.heading: The weather, month by month
months.sub: Colombo is on the west coast, so it gets the south-west monsoon: driest from December to March, wettest in October and November.

blocks.label: Dec – Mar
blocks.title: Dry & busy
blocks.text: The driest months — January and February see rain on only about five days each. Peak season: book hotels and Ministry of Crab well ahead.

blocks.label: Apr – Jun
blocks.title: Hot, then the monsoon
blocks.text: Hot and sticky, with the first monsoon rains peaking in May. Mid-April is Sinhala & Tamil New Year; Vesak falls at the May full moon.

blocks.label: Jul – Aug
blocks.title: A drier lull
blocks.text: The rain eases to well under half of May’s — still showers, but plenty of dry days. The Vel festival procession usually runs down Galle Road around now.

blocks.label: Sep – Nov
blocks.title: The wettest
blocks.text: October and November are the wettest months, with rain on more than half the days in October. Fewer visitors; Deepavali falls in October or November.

onTheWay.heading: Worth stopping for
onTheWay.sub: These are on the drives out of Colombo, not in the city. Your driver can stop — just ask.
onTheWay.note: Stops are free on a Ceylon Hop transfer — the link opens WhatsApp with the stop already typed, and we tell the driver.

stops.name: Cadjugama cashew stalls
stops.text: A village of roadside stalls that has sold cashews to passing travellers for over a century — “cadju” is cashew, “gama” is village. Taste before you buy.
stops.wa: Hi Ceylon Hop — on my Colombo → Kandy transfer, could we stop at the Cadjugama cashew stalls? (From your Colombo guide.)

stops.km: To Galle · coast road, about 42 km
stops.name: Kalutara Bodhiya
stops.text: A white, hollow dagoba by the Kalutara bridge — step inside to see 74 painted panels of the Buddha’s life. Shoes off, shoulders and knees covered. It’s on the coast road, not the expressway, so ask us to go that way.
stops.wa: Hi Ceylon Hop — on my Colombo → Galle transfer, could we take the coast road and stop at Kalutara Bodhiya? (From your Colombo guide.)

eatSub: From century-old bakeries to the island’s most famous crab. Small local places are cash only.

eat.name: Ministry of Crab · Shang Palace · Nuga Gama
eat.text: Ministry of Crab, in the Old Dutch Hospital, is consistently rated among Asia’s best — order the garlic chilli or pepper crab, and book well ahead. Shang Palace at the Shangri-La for Cantonese with a sea view; Nuga Gama at the Cinnamon Grand for Sri Lankan food in a recreated village under a banyan tree. Ministry of Crab doesn’t hold tables after 15 minutes.

eat.name: Green Cabin · Pilawoos · Perera & Sons
eat.text: Green Cabin on Galle Road for rice and curry and its famous lamprais; Hotel de Pilawoos for kottu at any hour — it never closes. For short eats — fish buns, patties, cutlets — Perera & Sons, the century-old bakery with a branch on every corner, or Bombay Sweet Mahal opposite the Red Mosque for samosas and sweets. Follow the local queue.

eat.name: Kopi Kade · Café Kumbuk · ITC Ratnadipa
eat.text: Kopi Kade for serious coffee, Café Kumbuk for a laid-back brunch with the locals (closed Tuesdays), Butter Boutique for cakes. For a proper afternoon tea, ITC Ratnadipa is the polished new one; Sapphyr Lounge at the Shangri-La does it daily with sea views. For gelato, Isle of Gelato at Colombo City Centre and One Galle Face.

eatCollector.title: Where did you eat well?
eatCollector.text: Tell us your favourite place in Colombo and we’ll check it out for the next traveller.
eatCollector.fine: A photo of the menu is even better.
eatCollector.wa: Hi Ceylon Hop — a place I ate well in Colombo:

staySub: Stay in Colombo 3 or 7 for the seafront and the best restaurants. Flight before about 8 AM? Skip the city traffic and sleep in Negombo, near the airport.

stay.name: Residence by Uga · Tintagel · Maniumpathy
stay.text: Residence by Uga Escapes, eleven suites in a townhouse near Gangaramaya with the acclaimed Rare restaurant; Paradise Road Tintagel, a heritage mansion in Cinnamon Gardens; Maniumpathy, eight rooms in a 1906 house in Borella. Taprobane House, by the sea in Colombo 3, is the smaller, quieter one.

stay.name: ITC Ratnadipa · Cinnamon Life · Galle Face Hotel
stay.text: The new towers — ITC Ratnadipa by Galle Face Green, with its spa, and Cinnamon Life at City of Dreams, with eight restaurants and two pools — or the Galle Face Hotel, the grand old dame since 1864, for the sunset bagpiper. Galle Face Hotel reviews have been mixed lately; go for the history and the Verandah.

stay.name: Clock Inn · Hangover Hostels · Colombo Beach Hostel
stay.text: Clock Inn on Galle Road in Kollupitiya, good for solo travellers and couples, with female-only dorms; Hangover Hostels, clean dorms and private rooms near Bambalapitiya. Colombo Beach Hostel, known for its family dinners, is a top pick for solo travellers. Colombo Beach Hostel is in Mount Lavinia — by the beach, but 30–40 minutes from the sights.

stayCollector.title: Stayed somewhere great?
stayCollector.text: Guesthouse, hostel, homestay — tell us and we’ll add the good ones here.
stayCollector.wa: Hi Ceylon Hop — a place I stayed and liked in Colombo:

items.a: Yes — at least one night, two if you like food and a night out. Most people land, sleep and leave, but the temples, Bawa’s architecture, Port City and the rooftop bars are reason enough to stay. Two days covers it all without rushing.

items.q: First or last night: Colombo or Negombo?
items.a: For a flight before about 8 AM, sleep in Negombo or by the airport — no city traffic between you and the terminal. With a day to spare, stay in Colombo and see it: the airport is about 50 minutes away, longer at rush hour.

items.q: Which area should I stay in?
items.a: Colombo 3 and 7 (Kollupitiya, Cinnamon Gardens): the seafront, the best restaurants and most of the big hotels. The Fort: the old buildings and the station, busy by day and quiet at night. Mount Lavinia: a beach suburb to the south, sleepier and further from everything. Negombo: your last night before an early flight.

In Pettah and the Fort, a guide earns the fee: the lanes start to make sense and the touts leave you alone. Walks run from tip-based to about USD 128 for a four-hour premium walk. Galle Face, the temples and the tower are easy on your own.

items.q: Where do I go out at night?
items.a: Colombo leans to rooftop bars and lounges more than big clubs. ON14, on the 14th floor of the Radisson (the old OZO), for the view; Park Street Mews for restaurants and bars with live music, good for hopping between; Taphouse by RnR in the Dutch Hospital for craft beer and bands; The Chiller Room for a relaxed, welcoming crowd; the Irish Bar & Grill on Park Street for pub food and the football. Book the rooftops at weekends. Want it quieter? A hotel lounge bar beats the clubs near Galle Face.

Every full moon is a public holiday. Expect a dry day: bars and shops stop selling alcohol, though some hotels serve their own guests. The National Museum and Ministry of Crab close. Check the date before you plan a big dinner.

items.q: Where do people go after Colombo?
items.a: South to Galle — about 2 h 15 down the expressway — or inland to Kandy, about 3 h 30. From May to September, the east coast is the beach in season. See the routes ↓

items.q: How long is the drive to the airport?
items.a: About 50 minutes from the city on the expressway, and an hour or more at rush hour. Aim to be at the terminal about three hours before an international flight — tell us your flight time and we’ll set the pickup.

Bandaranaike International has started letting passengers check in up to four hours before departure, and has self-service kiosks and bag drop. Useful if your hotel checkout is at noon and your flight is in the evening.

items.q: Where do I get a SIM card?
items.a: At the mobile-network counters in the arrivals hall. Sort it before you leave the terminal, so the app and the maps work from the start.

PickMe is the main app, for cars and tuk-tuks; Uber works mostly in Colombo. At the airport, check the plate and the driver match the app before you get in. Or book with us, and your driver meets you at arrivals.

items.q: Is there a bus from the airport?
items.a: Yes — route 187, an air-conditioned bus along the expressway to the Colombo Fort bus stand. It leaves from the outer porch of the departure terminal.

Hot and sticky all year, so it feels warmer than the numbers. Plan the middle of the day indoors — a museum, a long lunch, the hotel pool.

• Loose cotton or linen
  • Shoulders and knees covered for temples
  • Shoes that slip off easily
  • A compact umbrella (Apr–Jun, Sep–Nov)

Your passport for Lotus Tower and any reserved train. A sarong or shawl — Pettah and Barefoot sell them — doubles as temple cover. Sunscreen, a hat, insect repellent for the evenings, a refillable bottle, and rupees for Pettah and the temples.

items.q: Is it a problem to have a Buddha tattoo?
items.a: It can be. Visible Buddha tattoos can get you refused entry to temples, or even deported. Keep them covered.

tips: The festival scam: a friendly, respectable-looking stranger says there’s a special temple festival today and flags you a tuk-tuk. There’s no festival — the ride ends at a gem shop. Smile and walk on.
Use ATMs inside banks or hotels — card fraud is a known problem. Bag-snatching from motorbikes happens too, so keep your bag on the side away from the road.
Carry cash for Pettah, the street food and the temples. Lotus Tower charges your card in rupees; the National Museum takes cards but prefers cash.
Tuk-tuks: book through PickMe or Uber so the fare is set, or agree the price before you get in.
Poya (full-moon) days: expect a dry day — some hotels serve their own guests. The National Museum and Ministry of Crab are closed.
Never pose with your back to a Buddha statue, at Gangaramaya or anywhere else.
Book Ministry of Crab ahead, especially December to March, and be on time: tables aren’t held after 15 minutes.
Mount Lavinia’s beach is for sunsets, not swimming: rip currents have pulled swimmers out, and lifeguards only work at busy times.
Drink-spiking and harassment in crowded places are both reported. Watch your drink at night, and in the Pettah crowds keep your wits about you.
Rush hour turns the 50-minute airport run into an hour or more. Tell us your flight time and we’ll plan the pickup around it.
Plugs are mostly the UK three-pin (type G), with some older round-pin sockets (D and M); 230 V. Bring a universal adapter — not every hostel has spares.
Public toilets are few. Plan around malls, hotels, cafés and restaurants.

ask.heading: Not sure about something?
ask.text: Lotus Tower slots, whether the Kandy train is running yet, where to sleep before an early flight — message us and we’ll check. That’s what we’re here for.
